Appellant, Nek Raj, has filed the present appeal, under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988,
as amended upto date, (hereinafter referred to as the 'M.V. Act'), against the award dated 28.12.2012, passed by learned Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Chamba H.P., (hereinafter referred to as the 'learned Tribunal'), in MAC Petition No.7 of 2012, titled as Nek Raj Versus National Insurance Company Limited & Another.

3. Brief facts, leading to filing of the present appeal, before this Court, may be summed up, as under:-
3.1.

The petitioner Nek Raj has filed the claim petition under Section 166 of the M.V.
Act, against the respondents, being insurer and owner-cum-driver of vehicle No.HP47-5500 (hereinafter referred to as the 'offending vehicle').
3.2
The claim petition has been filed on the grounds that on 9.9.2011, at about 8.45 a.m., petitioner was on his way to Parel from Udaipur, on his motorcycle bearing No.HP48-9936.
He has to drop his son in a private School at Parel.
He was driving the motorcycle very carefully, on the left side of the road.

In the meanwhile, the offending vehicle, being driven by respondent No.2, in a rash and negligent manner,
had come there from the opposite direction and he could not control the vehicle and hit the motorcycle.
Due to this, the petitioner had sustained injuries on his left leg.
3.3 Thereafter, the petitioner was taken to Civil Hospital, Chamba, for treatment from where, he was taken to Swami Hari Giri Hospital, Kakira, District Chamba.
The petitioner remain admitted there from 9.9.2011 to 15.9.2011.
After getting discharge from the Hospital, the petitioner confined to bed for about 21 days.

. 
3.4 According to the petitioner, he has spent a sum of Rs.45,000/- on his treatment.

The information regarding the accident was given to the police of Police Station,

2 Chamba, where, FIR No.224/2011, dated 9.9.2011, was registered.

sentences.text: 3.5. On all these submissions, the petitioner has prayed rate of 12% per annum.
r to for the compensation of Rs.1,45,000/-, along with interest, at the 4.
When put to notice, claim petition has been contested by respondents.

5. Respondent No.1-Insurance Company has taken the preliminary objections that the petition is not maintainable;
petition is bad for non-joinder of necessary party, as the owner and insurer of Motor Cycle No.HP48-9936 have not been impleaded in the present case.

6. Apart from this, the Insurance Company has taken the plea that the accident, in question, had taken place due to the negligence of the petitioner himself, as such, he is not liable for any compensation.
7. Contesting the petition on merits, the factual position, as asserted in the claim petition, has been denied.

8. Respondent No.2, who is the owner-cum-driver of the offending vehicle, filed his reply, in which,
the factum of .
registration of FIR against him, has not been disputed, but, according to him, the same has been lodged on false and twisted facts.

Elaborating his stand, it is his case that the accident, in question,
had taken place due to the rash and negligent driving of the petitioner himself.
9. Perusal of the reply filed by respondent No.2, shows that factual position has not been disputed by him, in this case.
10. Thus, both the respondents had prayed for dismissal of the claim petition.

11. Petitioner has also filed rejoinder to the replies filed by the respondents by denying the preliminary objections, as well as, the stand, by virtue of which, the factual position has been controverted by reasserting that of the petition.
12. From the pleadings of the parties, learned Tribunal has framed the following issues vide order dated 16.8.2012:

1. Whether the petitioner Nek Raj sustained injuries during the rash and negligent driving of respondent No.2 while driving vehicle no.HP47- 5500 on 9.9.2011 near Hotel Royal Dream at Parel, Tehsil and District Chamba as alleged?

13.

A perusal of the record shows that on 16.8.2012, an application under Section 170 of M.V. Act,
moved by the Insurance Company, has also been dismissed by the learned Tribunal.
14. After framing the issues, the parties to the claim petition, have adduced their respective evidence.

15. After closure of the evidence and hearing of learned counsel for the parties, the learned Tribunal has dismissed the petition, mainly on the ground that the petitioner himself was not having a valid and effective driving licence to drive the vehicle involved in the accident, as such, by relying on the decision of this Court in New Assurance Company Vs. Tika Ram & Others, 2011(2) Him.L.R., 879,
the petitioner has been held to be not entitled for any compensation.
16.

sentences.text:
Against the said decision, the present appeal has been filed before this Court, challenging the award passed by .
the learned Tribunal, by virtue of which, his claim petition has been dismissed.

17. The award has been assailed on the ground that the learned Tribunal has failed to appreciate the evidence led by the petitioner, that he has sustained injuries in the accident, which had taken place due to rash and negligent driving of respondent No.2.

The findings of learned Tribunal has also been assailed on the ground that he was wrongly non-suited on account of the fact that he was not holding a valid and effective driving licence, whereas, according to the petitioner, it was not in issue in the said claim petition.
However, the Insurance Company has proved/probablized that the petitioner was not having a valid and effective driving licence, at the time of accident.

18. Similarly, the findings of the learned Tribunal qua the fact that the petitioner has received reimbursement of the amount, which he has spent on his treatment, is also not sustainable, in the eyes of law.
Elaborating his stand, the findings have been further assailed on the ground that he has received only a sum of Rs.10,026/- as medical reimbursement, in this case.

sentences.text: On all these submissions, a prayer has been made to set aside the award and allow the petition.

The prayer so made, has been opposed by the learned counsel for the respondents on the ground that the learned Tribunal has rightly dismissed the petition, as respondent No.2, was not having the valid and effective driving licence.
21. The proceedings under the M.V. Act, are summary in nature, where, the liability of the tort-feaser can be fixed, on the principle of preponderance of probability.
Strict Rules of Evidence Act are not applicable to the summary proceedings under the M.V. Act.

The relief under the M.V.
Act
, is based upon tortious liability.

Since, the M.V. Act is the beneficial piece of legislation, as such,
while deciding the claim petition, the endevaour of the Tribunal should be to award 'just compensation'.
22.
Learned Tribunal, in the present case, has not framed any issue, with regard to the effect that the petitioner himself was negligent.

The issues were framed in the presence of parties and it has specifically been held by the learned Tribunal that the issues are read over and explained to the parties and no other issue arises or claimed.
23. The learned Tribunal has non-suited the petitioner, in this case, only on the ground that he was not having the driving .
licence, while deciding issues No.1 and 3.

Relevant para 16 of the judgment, passed by learned Tribunal, is reproduced as under:-
"16.
The moot question thus is whether the petitioner was legally entitled to drive a two wheeler while holding a licence only to drive a LMV.

In this behalf, the respondents have placed reliance on a judgment of our own Hon'ble High court titled as New Assurance Company Vs. Tika Ram & Others, 2011(2) Him.L.R., 879, to contend that the petitioner was not entitled to any compensation as he himself was not competent to drive the motor cycle"
24.

sentences.text: In this case the petitioner has proved, the copy of FIR, as Ex.PW-1/A, by examining HHC Karam Singh, PW-1.
This witness has admitted that neither he has registered the FIR, nor investigated the case.
At the same time, he has also admitted that petitioner is working in their department.

25. Petitioner Nek Raj appeared in the witness-box, as PW-5 and filed his affidavit Ex.PW-5/A,
which is based upon the averments made in the claim petition.
In cross-examination, he has admitted that he was driving the offending vehicle by denying the suggestion that he was not having a driving licence.
Lastly, he has denied the suggestion that the accident, in question, has taken place due to his rash and negligent driving.

sentences.text: 26. Similarly, in the cross-examination by respondent No.2, petitioner has denied all the suggestions, which have been put to him, in order to probablize the stand of respondent No.2.
He has admitted the fact that his son was pillion rider on the motorcycle, at the time of accident.
27. Except this evidence, there is no other evidence on the record.
From this evidence no inference can be drawn that the respondents have probablize their defence.

Respondent No.2, who has taken this defence that the accident, in question, had taken place due to the rash and negligent driving of the petitioner himself, has not bothered to appear in the witness-box to probablize his defence.

28. Once a party fails to appear, in the witness-box to depose, as per his case, then an adverse inference is to be drawn, unless and until, the factual position has been admitted by the opposite party or he could probablize the same from the cross-examination of the witnesses.
29. Pleadings are the backbone of the case.
Factum of registration of FIR has been mentioned in para 9.
Respondent No.1, has admitted the registration of the FIR by pleading that the said para needs no reply, being a matter of record.

30. Similarly, the person, who was driving the offending vehicle has also admitted the factum of registration of FIR, but, .
according to him, the same has been lodged on the false and twisted facts.
His reply is totally silent about the fact, whether he has made any representation to the higher authorities regarding the false registration of the case.

In the ordinary course of event, had a false FIR been registered against him,
he would have lodged the complaint or made representation to the higher authorities, in this regard.
Nothing of the sort has been done by respondent No.2, in this case.
31. The view of the learned Tribunal is not sustainable in the judicial scrutiny by this Court, in view of the discussion made above.
Merely, on the ground of not having the driving licence, no inference of negligence could be drawn against the petitioner.

While holding so, this Court is being guided by the decision of Hon'ble Apex Court in CIVIL APPEAL No.22966 OF 2017, titled as SRI DINESH KUMAR. J. @ DINESH J, Versus NATIONAL INSURANCE CO. LTD & ORS, relevant para 8, are reproduced here has under:-
"8.

We are in agreement with the submission which has been urged on behalf of the appellant that plea of contributory negligence was accepted purely .

sentences.text:
Once the finding that there was contributory negligence on the part of the appellant is held to be without any basis,
the second aspect which weighed both with the tribunal and the High Court, that the appellant had not produced the driving licence, would be of no relevance.

This aspect has been considered in a judgment of this Court in Sudhir Kumar (supra) where it was held as follows :
"9.
If a person drives a vehicle without a licence, he commits an offence.
The same, by itself, in our opinion, may not lead to a finding of negligence as regards the accident.
It has been held by the courts below that it was the driver of the mini truck who was driving rashly and negligently.
It is one thing to say that the appellant was not possessing any licence but no finding of fact has been arrived at that he was driving the two-wheeler rashly and negligently.

If he was not driving rashly and negligently which contributed to the accident, we fail to see as to how, only because he was not having a licence, he would be held to be guilty of contributory negligence...

10. The matter might have been different if by reason of his rash and negligent driving, the accident had taken place."
32.
The contents of the FIR Ex.PW-1/A, assumes significance.

The same has been registered on the statement of petitioner Nek Raj, in which, he has specifically alleged that the accident, in question,
has taken place due to the rash and negligent driving of respondent No.2.
.
33.

Although, the proceedings under the M.V. Act, are summary in nature, but, this does not mean that the plea, which has been taken by the respondents, in their reply, in this case, can be taken into consideration.
Merely, pleading these facts does not suffice that the petitioner was negligent.

When a specific stand has been taken by respondent No.2, in the reply, that the accident had taken place due to rash and negligent driving of the petitioner, then it was incumbent upon him to prove or probablize the said fact by leading evidence or on the basis of the cross-examination of the petitioner.
34. Admittedly, respondent No.2 has not bothered to appear in the witness-box to depose, as per the averments made in the reply.

Even otherwise, simply giving the suggestion to the petitioner Nek Raj,
qua the fact that the accident, in question, has taken place, due to his rash and negligent driving,
does not ipso facto prove this fact.

35. In such situation, the findings of the learned Tribunal, regarding dis-entitlement of the petitioner for compensation, simply on account of the fact that he was not having a valid and effective driving licence to drive the vehicle, which he in fact was driving, is not sustainable in the eyes of law and the same are liable to be reversed.
Consequently, the same are reversed.

38. According to the affidavit, filed by the petitioner, in his examination-in-chief, after the accident,
he was firstly taken to Civil Hospital, Chamba, from where, he was referred to Swami Hari Giri Hospital, where he remain admitted from 9.9.2011 to 15.9.2011.
He has specifically deposed that he has spent Rs.45,000/- on his treatment.

To prove this fact, he has examined PW-2, Goldi Rana,
Pharmacist from Swami Hari Giri Hospital, Kakira, who has also deposed, on oath, that injured remain admitted in their Hospital from 9.9.2011 to 15.9.2011.

He has proved the admission form as Ex.PW-2/A and cash memos Ex.PW-2/B-1 to Ex.PW-B-11.
39. PW-3, Tilak Raj, has stated that his vehicle was hired by the injured (petitioner) for his to and fro journey for Hospital.
.
He has also proved the bills Ex.PW-3/A to Ex.PW-3/C.

In such situation, the entitlement of the petitioner for compensation is adjudicated, as under:-
1.

NON PECUNIARY DAMAGES:
(a) PAIN AND SUFFERING:
40.

The petitioner, after the accident, was firstly taken to Civil Hospital, Chamba, from where, he was referred to Swami Hari Giri Hospital-cum-Research Centre, Kakira,
where, as per the document Ex.PW-2/A, he was admitted on 9.9.2011 and was discharged on 15.9.2011.

(b) LOSS OF ENJOYMENT OF LIFE:
41.
As per the petitioner, he remained on leave for 21 days.

The petitioner is working as constable in Police Department and in the absence of any document to prove that he was forced to take his earned leave, it can be presumed that he was on medical Nek Raj vs National Insurance Company on 19 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199456337/

(c) SHORTEN EXPECTANCY OF LIFE:
42.

There is no evidence on the record to prove or to .
suggest that due to the accident or injuries sustained by him, his life span has been shortened.

2. PECUNIARY DAMAGES:
(a) MEDICAL EXPENSES:
43.
Although, the petitioner is a Police constable and an employee of Government of Himachal Pradesh.

He has taken a specific stand in the appeal that he has received only a sum of Rs.10,026/-
under the head, medical reimbursement, whereas he has proved the medical bills Ex.PW-2/B-1 to PW-B-11, the total of which comes to Rs.25,088/-.
Out of which amount, a sum of Rs.10,026/- is liable to be deducted, which the petitioner has received as medical reimbursement.
Thus, the petitioner is entitled to Rs.15062/-, as compensation under this head.

(b) TRAVELLING EXPENSES:
44.
Considering the statement of PW-3 and the documents Ex.PW-3/A to Ex.PW-3/C proved by him, the petitioner is held entitled to Rs.1800+Rs.2550+Rs.2550= Rs.6900/-, as compensation, under this head.

(c) SPECIAL DIET AND ATTENDANT CHARGES:-
45.
Considering the period of Hospitalization, during which, the petitioner could not attend the office, the said period comes to about 30 days.

During that period, the petitioner might have required the services of an attendant and special .
diet.
Considering the said period, it would be just and appropriate for this Court to award a sum of Rs.10,000/-, as compensation, under this head.
